nSymbolic	AI

qAI	systems	that	represent	knowledge	as	symbolsand	manipulate	them	with

Transduction Problem
nDefinition
qIn	symbolic	AI,	an	agent	reasons	using	symbols(logic,	rules,	representations).
qThe	transduction	problemrefers	to	the	challenge	of	converting	raw	sensory	data	
(from	the	real	world)	into	symbolic	representationsthat	the	agent	can	use.
nExample：
n IF	object	=	apple	THEN	caneat
n But	how	does	the	agent	know	from	raw	camera	pixels	that	“this	is	an	apple”?
n The	conversion	from	pixels	→	“apple”	symbolis	the	transduction	problem.
nWhy	It’s	Hard
n The	world	is	continuous,	noisy,	and	ambiguous.
n Symbolic	systems	expect	clean,	discrete	symbols.
n Example	challenges:
qVision:	mapping	millions	of	pixel	values	to	objects.
qSpeech:	mapping	waveforms	into	words/symbols.
9

Heuristic Search
Transduction Problem
nLimitations:
qSymbolic	systems	worked	fine	in	abstract	domains	(math,	logic,	medical	diagnosis	
with	structured	data).
qBut	they	struggled	in	perception-heavy	tasks(vision,	speech,	robotics).
qThis	was	one	reason	symbolic	AI	faced	limitations	→	paving	the	way	for	statistical	
&	learning-based	AI(which	can	process	raw	data	directly).
nToday,	machine	learning	(especially	deep	learning)addresses	the	transduction	
problem	by	learning	mappings	from	raw	data	→	features	→	symbols	(or	decisions).
nHybrid	approaches:	neuro-symbolic	AItries	to	combine	learning	(for	transduction)	
with	symbolic	reasoning	(for	logic).

Symbolic Reasoning
nDefinition
q Symbolic	reasoning	=	manipulating	symbols	that	represent	concepts,	objects,	and	rules.
q Follows	logic-based	rulesto	derive	new	facts	from	known	facts.
nExample
q Rule:	If	X	is	human,	then	X	is	mortal.
q Fact:	Frankis	human.
q Reasoning:	Therefore,	Frankis	mortal.
nStrengths
q Transparent	reasoning	(easy	to	explain).
q Effective	in	structured	domains	(math,	law,	medicine).
nWeaknesses
q Struggles	with	uncertainty,	ambiguity,	perception.
q Requires	manual	knowledge	engineering.

Simulated Annealing
▪ Simulated Annealing = physics inspired twist 
on random walk
▪ Escape from local optima by accepting, with a 
probability that decreases during the search, 
also moves that are worse than the current 
solution (going downhill!)
▪ Stochastic, solution-improvement 
metaheuristic for global optimization

Simulated Annealing
▪ Basic ideas:
❑ like hill-climbing identify the quality of the local improvements
❑ instead of picking the best move, pick one randomly 
❑ say the change in objective function is d
❑ if d is positive, then move to that state
❑ otherwise: 
move to this state with probability proportional to d
thus: worse moves (very large negative d) are executed less often
❑ however, there is always a chance of escaping from local maxima
❑ over time, make it less likely to accept locally bad moves
❑ (Can also make the size of the move random as well, i.e., allow “large” steps 
in state space)

this is like simulated annealing
▪ Annealing = physical process of cooling a liquid or metal 
until particles achieve a certain frozen crystal state

Elbow Method

▪ First of all, compute the sum of squared error 
(SSE) for some values of k (for example 2, 4, 6, 
8, etc.). 
▪ The SSE is defined as the sum of the squared 
distance between each member of the cluster 
and its centroid. 
Elbow Method

▪ If you plot k against the SSE, you will see that the 
error decreases as k gets larger; 
▪ This is because when the number of clusters 
increases, they should be smaller, so distortion is 
also smaller. 
▪ The idea of the elbow method is to choose the k at 
which the SSE decreases abruptly. This produces 
an "elbow effect" in the graph
